title: Seizure Prediction
answer: Seizure prediction is the attempt to forecast an epileptic seizure before it happens, using brain signals and other physiological data. It sits within neuroinformatics and the brain, where it draws on electroencephalography, intracranial recordings, and wearable sensors. Unlike seizure detection, which identifies a seizure already in progress, prediction aims to give a warning window of minutes to hours. The field is part of The AI Physician, a broader effort to bring machine learning into clinical care. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Seizure prediction is the attempt to forecast an epileptic seizure before it happens, using brain signals and other physiological data. It sits within neuroinformatics and the brain, where it draws on electroencephalography, intracranial recordings, and wearable sensors. Unlike seizure detection, which identifies a seizure already in progress, prediction aims to give a warning window of minutes to hours. The field is part of The AI Physician, a broader effort to bring machine learning into clinical care. Among the 1000 medical AI models tracked on this site, a subset addresses seizure prediction, though most remain research prototypes rather than approved clinical tools.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Seizure prediction systems run on a mix of patient-worn sensors, bedside monitors, and implanted devices. The core input is usually continuous electroencephalography, sometimes supplemented by heart rate, accelerometry, or electrodermal activity. Signal processing and feature extraction often happen on a local edge device to keep latency low, while model training and updates may use hospital servers or cloud infrastructure. Some systems are designed for closed-loop use, where a prediction triggers a warning or a neurostimulation response. Power, bandwidth, and comfort constraints shape what can be worn or implanted.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with long recordings of brain activity, often from patients undergoing presurgical evaluation or wearing ambulatory EEG. Engineers and clinicians label seizure onset times, then split the data into preictal, ictal, and interictal periods. Models are trained to distinguish the preictal state from normal background activity, using architectures such as convolutional or recurrent neural networks. Because seizures are rare events, the data are highly imbalanced, and performance is judged by sensitivity, false alarm rate, and time in warning. Validation usually starts retrospectively and then moves to prospective, patient-specific testing.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Seizure prediction touches sensitive neurological data, so consent, de-identification, and data governance are central. Provenance matters because a model's warning depends on the quality and origin of the EEG it was trained on, and version control is needed for clinical accountability. Regulatory pathways are still emerging, as most seizure prediction systems are not cleared for independent clinical use. Across medical AI generally, this site tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits, which shows the legal exposure when automated systems fail. The site also tracks 219 compliance and regulation pages, reflecting the growing body of rules that surround patient data and clinical software.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward closed-loop systems that combine prediction with responsive neurostimulation or drug delivery. Researchers are working on models that generalize across patients, rather than requiring a new model for each person. Wearable and smartphone-linked sensors may make long-term monitoring more practical outside the hospital. Regulatory science is developing ways to evaluate prediction accuracy and safety before widespread adoption. The long-term goal is a reliable warning that gives patients time to act, though prediction is not yet standard care.
